demos.description: Agent picker — browse and activate a built-in agent

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Now type /agent to browse your custom agents.
A picker opens. Create a new agent or learn more about custom agents.
Use the arrow keys to move, Enter to select, Escape to cancel.
Think of it as a roster of specialist helpers.
Let's start by opening Copilot CLI.
Type /chronicle standup to summarize your recent work.
Copilot now builds a standup update from your recent session history.
It proposes checking recent git commits, and asks your permission before running.
You can approve once, approve for the repo, or tell it to do something else.
Chronicle turns your history into a ready-made standup.

steps.type: /delegate write unit tests for the app

narration.text: First, open Copilot CLI.
Type /delegate followed by the task you want handed off.
Copilot checks your repo for uncommitted changes.
It asks to send this to GitHub.
Hand work off to a remote agent.

demos.command: /fleet run all test suites in parallel

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /fleet followed by a task you want run in parallel.
Fleet mode is deployed, and Copilot thinks about how to split the work.
It first runs a shell command to check which test scripts exist.
The result: this project has no test suites, so it suggests running type-check and lint instead.
Fleet shines when a job can be split into parallel subagents.
First, start Copilot CLI.
Type /ide to connect Copilot to your editor.
It can auto-connect to VS Code, but no IDE workspace is open here.
Link your editor so the CLI sees your code.

demos.command: /research NEXTJS app deployment option pros and cons

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /research followed by the topic you want investigated.
Copilot starts a deep research run and begins thinking about the question.
It drafts a plan with key areas, then dispatches parallel subagents to research each.
Subagents keep researching while the status line shows progress.
When it finishes you get a structured report with citations.
First, open Copilot CLI.
Type /sidekicks list to see your running sidekick agents.
A panel lists your sidekicks. Right now it says no sidekicks.
Sidekicks are helper agents beside you.
Start by launching Copilot CLI.
Type /tasks to see what is running in the background.
A Tasks panel lists background subagents and shell commands, both empty here.
Use it to manage background work.

demos.description: Authenticate — select GitHub.com, then show device code

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /login to sign in to Copilot.
Pick GitHub.com or GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
It shows a one-time code to enter on GitHub's device page.
Enter it in your browser to finish.

demos.description: Show current user, then preview /logout (cancelled safely)

narration.text: First, start Copilot CLI.
Before logging out, check who you are with /user show.
It greets you by the account you are signed in as.
Now type /logout to sign out.
Press Enter to sign out.

demos.description: Show current user then list all authenticated accounts

narration.text: First, open Copilot CLI.
Type /user show to see which account is active.
Copilot greets you with your signed-in account.
Now type /user list to see every authenticated account.
Your accounts are listed.
Handy for switching accounts.

demos.command: /ask what does --no-ff mean in git merge?

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /ask followed by a quick side question, like what no-ff means in git merge.
Copilot thinks, then answers in a temporary side panel.
It explains that no-ff forces a merge commit, and sketches the branch history.
Press escape to dismiss it. Like a private aside, it never joins the main history.
Let's start by launching Copilot CLI.
Now type /clear to start fresh.
The screen resets to a clean slate.
Like a new browser tab.

demos.command: /new help me refactor the auth module

narration.text: Launch Copilot CLI to get started.
Type /new followed by an opening prompt, like help me refactor the auth module.
Like a fresh browser tab: old history is cleared and your prompt starts a new chat.
Copilot thinks, then searches the repo for anything auth related.
It answers there is no auth module here, and asks what you meant.
First, start Copilot CLI.
Type /search and a keyword, such as JWT.
The search bar opens. It says no results, since this fresh chat never mentioned JWT.
Like Ctrl+F for a chat.
First, launch Copilot CLI. Experimental mode is needed for this one.
Type /every, an interval, then a prompt: every 30 minutes, summarize recent file changes.
Copilot confirms it will repeat every 30 minutes.
Like a recurring calendar reminder.

demos.description: Refine a rough prompt into a clear, well-structured one
demos.command: /refine so basically i want like a button that does the thing with the files maybe sort them

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /refine followed by a rough, stream of consciousness idea, full of filler words and maybes.
Don't worry about the wording. Just dump your thought, then press enter.
Copilot refines it into a clear, concise request, now sitting in the input box.
You can review or edit it before sending, so the final prompt is precise.
Like an editor polishing your draft before it goes out.
First, launch Copilot CLI. This command needs experimental mode.
Type /after with a delay, then a prompt: after 10 minutes, check if the build finished.
Copilot confirms it will run once after that delay.
Like a one-off timer.

demos.description: Ask copilot a quick question then rewind the last turn with /undo

steps.type: what is the latest LTS version of Node.js?

narration.text: Launch Copilot CLI first.
Ask Copilot something first. Here, we ask for the latest LTS version of Node.js.
Copilot thinks, then runs a web search for the answer.
While it works, type /undo to rewind the last turn.
It is queued; once done, a rewind picker appears.

demos.description: Create a GitHub fork of the current repository

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI in your project.
Type /branch, an alias of /fork, to fork the current session.
Copilot confirms the fork, and the new copy of the session opens, ready to use.
Think of it as a safe copy to experiment in.
Let's start by opening Copilot CLI.
Now type /diff to review your uncommitted changes.
Diff Mode opens and Copilot looks for your unstaged changes.
Fast orientation before a review.

demos.description: Create a GitHub fork of the current repository

narration.text: Begin by launching Copilot CLI.
Now type /fork to make a copy of the current session.
Copilot reports the new forked session, and you are now working inside that copy.
Like clicking Fork: your own copy, original untouched.

demos.command: /plan add a favorites feature to bookmark commands in the cheatsheet app

narration.text: First, start Copilot CLI.
Type /plan, then describe what to build, like adding a favorites feature.
Copilot will outline a plan first, and wait for your approval before changing any files.
After you press Enter, Copilot thinks about the request.
It explores the project, listing folders and reading key files.
This research comes first, so the plan fits your actual code.
Like asking a contractor for a quote first.
First, fire up Copilot CLI.
Type /pr create to open a pull request with an AI-written description.
Copilot starts thinking about your pull request.
It checks your branch, changes, and commits.
Copilot asks permission first; pick Yes to let it run.
Like a PR dashboard in your terminal.

demos.description: Run security review agent on current diff

narration.text: To begin, launch Copilot CLI.
Now type /security-review to scan your changes for vulnerabilities.
Copilot starts a security review that analyzes for vulnerabilities.
A dedicated security agent starts inspecting your local changes.
It runs git commands to see what changed and read repo instructions.
Like a security auditor for your PR.
First, open Copilot CLI.
Type /review to run the built-in code review agent.
Copilot thinks about your request.
It decides to launch a code review agent.
The agent starts in the background on your changes.
Copilot waits for the agent to finish. Like an expert review before you push.

demos.description: Create a new git worktree, leaving uncommitted changes in the current session

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /worktree to start a parallel branch in a fresh git worktree.
Copilot starts creating a name for the new worktree.
Your uncommitted work stays put in the old session.

demos.description: Create a new git worktree and carry uncommitted changes into it

narration.text: Start by opening Copilot CLI.
Type /move followed by a task, like fix the login redirect.
It also carries your uncommitted changes.
Copilot names the branch from your task and prepares a new worktree.
Like moving your desk to a new room.

demos.description: Open the current session in VS Code

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /code to hand this session over to VS Code.
Copilot closes and prints a summary with a resume command.
Same session, now in VS Code.

demos.description: Add src directory to the allowed list

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Now type /add-dir, followed by the folder you want to allow.
Copilot suggests matching folders as you type the path.
Allowing a folder lets Copilot read and modify files in it.

demos.description: Enable all permissions then verify status

narration.text: To start, open Copilot CLI.
Type /allow-all on to turn on every permission at once.
Tool, path, and URL requests are now approved automatically.
Let's verify by running /allow-all show.
Copilot reports that all permissions are enabled.
Use it only in trusted setups.
Let's start by launching Copilot CLI.
Type /cd and a path to change directory.
Copilot suggests folders as you type the path.
It works just like the shell cd command.
First, start Copilot CLI.
Type /cwd to see which directory you are working in.
Copilot prints the current working directory.
Give it a path and it moves there too.
Begin by launching Copilot CLI.
Type /env to inspect everything Copilot loaded.
It lists MCP servers, skills, and plugins.
Like printenv for Copilot.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /keep-alive busy to stop your machine sleeping while Copilot works.
Copilot confirms sleep is blocked while the agent works.
Great for long-running tasks.
To begin, open Copilot CLI.
Type /list-dirs to see which folders Copilot may access.
It prints a numbered list of the allowed directories.
Use /add-dir to allow more folders.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Loop is experimental, so enable that mode first.
Copilot restarts with it enabled.
Now type /loop, an interval, and the command to repeat.
Copilot confirms the schedule, running every hour.
Like a calendar event for AI tasks.
Start by launching Copilot CLI.
Type /reset-allowed-tools to clear every approval you've granted.
Copilot confirms session approvals and allow-all were reset.
Copilot will ask again.
Let's launch Copilot CLI.
Type /permissions to choose how strictly Copilot asks for approval.
A picker opens: manual, assisted, or allow all.
Choose how strict approvals should be.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /settings to open the settings editor.
One screen lists every setting and its value.
Edit them here, no JSON files needed.
To begin, open Copilot CLI.
Type /statusline to customize the bar at the bottom.
Toggle items like branch, context used, and agent.
A preview shows your footer.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /streamer-mode to toggle hiding of secrets like API keys.
Copilot confirms the streamer mode state.
Use it when streaming or sharing your screen.
Let's launch Copilot CLI.
Type /terminal-setup to configure multiline input keys.
Here, Copilot reports the terminal is unsupported.
Run it in VS Code or Windows Terminal.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /sandbox to see how Copilot is isolated.
Tabs cover credentials, filesystem, and network access.
See exactly what Copilot can reach.

demos.description: View or change persistent CLI defaults, e.g. default model

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /config model to change your default AI model.
Choose the default model for future sessions.
These defaults stick across sessions.
Let's start Copilot CLI.
Type /voice on to dictate prompts instead of typing them.
The first time, Copilot asks to download a voice runtime.
Then talk to Copilot hands-free.

demos.description: Open the GitHub app or browser fallback

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI in your terminal.
Type /app to open this session in the GitHub app.
It shows a link to download the GitHub app.
A doorway to a visual workspace.
Let's start by launching Copilot CLI.
Type /bug to report a problem.
Choose a survey, a bug report, or a feature request.
Same as /feedback.
First, open Copilot CLI.
Type /changelog last 2 to see the two most recent releases.
Copilot prints the latest release notes with recent features and fixes.
Catch up on what is new.
Launch Copilot CLI to begin.
Type /feedback to share thoughts on the CLI.
Choose a private survey, a bug report, or a feature request.
Only the survey is private.

demos.description: Show help for all slash commands

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /help.
It lists shortcuts, like @ for files.
Your quick reference card.
Open Copilot CLI inside the repository you want to set up.
Type /init to have Copilot learn your project.
Copilot starts thinking, then explores the repository structure.
It lists folders, searches for existing instruction files, and reads files like the readme.
Now it starts creating a copilot-instructions file from what it learned.
Run /init once per repo to teach Copilot your project.
First, start Copilot CLI.
Type /update to upgrade.
Copilot checks GitHub for the latest release.
It then shows the changelog for that version.
One command keeps you current.

demos.description: Show AI-credit limits and predict session usage

narration.text: Launch Copilot CLI to get started.
Type /limits predict to see a suggested spending cap for this session.
Limits are opt-in: a soft cap on AI credits for this session.
It suggests a limit from similar past sessions.
Keeps credit use in check.
First, fire up Copilot CLI.
Type /usage to see your session usage.
You get an activity chart plus changes and AI units used.
Your session dashboard.
Start by launching Copilot CLI.
Type /version to see which version you have.
It shows your installed version and update status.
A quick health check.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /instructions to see which instruction files are loaded.
It lists loaded files like AGENTS.md, each with a checkbox.
See which rules are shaping Copilot.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /plugins to open the interactive plugins dashboard.
Tabs for Installed, Online and Marketplace.
Like an IDE extension manager.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /plugin list to see which plugins are installed.
No plugins yet, plus steps to add a marketplace and install one.
Like an extension marketplace.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /skills list to see the custom skills available.
Skills found are listed, here one built-in skill with a description.
A library of reusable macros.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /lsp show to check your language servers.
It shows the LSP server status and your config file.
LSP gives Copilot code intelligence.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /mcp show to see your MCP servers.
It lists built-in servers like GitHub and your config file.
MCP adds tools to Copilot.

demos.description: Ask a question to build history, then compact it

steps.type: what is the difference between git merge and git rebase?

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Let's build some history by asking about git merge versus rebase.
Copilot thinks, then writes its answer, which now takes up context space.
Long chats fill the context window, so type /compact to summarize it.
Copilot starts condensing the conversation into a short summary, keeping key context.
Use it when a long chat fills your context window.
First, open Copilot CLI.
Type /context to see how full the context window is.
A grid shows token use: system, messages, free space, and buffer.
Like a fuel gauge.
Let's launch Copilot CLI first.
Type /rename followed by a new name for this session.
Here the name describes a GitHub Actions task.
Copilot confirms the session was renamed.
Clear names make sessions easy to find.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /resume to jump back into an earlier session.
A list of past sessions shows each summary, type, status, and last modified time.
Choose one to continue where you left off.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /session info to see details about the current session.
It shows the session ID, duration, and directory.
A session snapshot.
Let's open Copilot CLI first.
Type /share gist to export this session to a secret GitHub gist.
Copilot uploads it and prints a link to the new gist.
Handy for sharing a session with a teammate.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /experimental show to list the experimental features.
It lists the features and warns they may be unstable.
Like beta features.

demos.description: Open model picker and select a different model

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /model with no arguments to open the picker.
A list of models appears. Arrow down to pick one, then press enter.
Now the session uses the new model.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /theme and pick a mode. Here we choose dim.
The color mode is now dim, applied right away.
Like an editor's dark mode switch.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /collect-debug-logs to bundle diagnostics for a bug report.
A session picker appears, listing local and remote sessions to choose from.
It is like Export logs in a crashed app: one bundle for support.

demos.description: Analyze session logs for errors and anomalies

narration.text: Let's start by launching Copilot CLI.
Type /diagnose, which analyzes your session logs for problems.
Right now it refuses: it needs at least one prompt sent first.
Chat first, then it opens the black-box recorder for what happened.

demos.description: Send a prompt then run diagnostic checks

steps.type: what is the latest LTS version of Node.js?

narration.text: First, launch Copilot CLI.
To have something to analyze, first ask a normal question.
Copilot thinks, then decides to search the web for the answer.
Now type /diagnosis to analyze this session.
It finishes the answer first, then reads the session log.
The report says Healthy: no errors found.
Like a health check in one command.

demos.description: Set a focused autopilot objective for the session

steps.type: /autopilot fix all TypeScript errors in src/

narration.text: First, launch Copilot. Loading is sped up.
Type /autopilot, followed by your goal. Here: fix all TypeScript errors in the source folder.
It first asks which permission mode to use.
We choose Allow All, so it can work uninterrupted.
Copilot is now locked onto the goal.
It defines success: zero TypeScript errors, with the build and lint passing.
Then it inspects the project: the git status, the TypeScript config, and the source files.
And it keeps going until the objective is met. Think of it like setting a GPS destination.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /exit when you are ready to leave.
Copilot closes and you are back at the shell.
A graceful exit, not a force kill.
Launch Copilot CLI first.
Type /quit, which does the same thing as /exit.
Copilot closes and you are back at the shell.
Both work, so use whichever feels natural.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /remote on to let another device steer this session.
Remote steering is on, with a link to connect.
Like a screenshare, perfect for pair programming.
First, launch Copilot CLI.
Type /restart to reload the CLI process while keeping your session.
Like restarting a browser without losing tabs: the process reloads fresh.
Here it printed resume hints, as no saved session matched.
